selection_rationale: The set covers the four sub_types: TT/Bantam studio and broadcast bays (Switchcraft StudioPatch 9625/6425, Bittree 969-A, Neutrik NPPA-TT-PT), 6.35 mm TRS project-studio bays (Samson S-Patch Plus, Neutrik NYS-SPP-L1), an XLR tie-line panel (Canare 162U-X21) and a 75-ohm video patchbay (Canare 32MD-ST). Each one shows a different way of choosing the normalling: a front screwdriver cam (Switchcraft EZ Norm), a front mini-toggle (Samson), shunts under the designation strips (Bittree), a reversible PCB card (Neutrik NYS), swappable pre-configured jack pairs and normalling bars (Neutrik NPPA), and a mode fixed by the fitted jack type (Canare). Between them they cover normalled, half-normalled (bottom and top row), non-normalled/isolated, parallel and switchable operation. All of these documents were read directly; the Behringer PX3000 was dropped because no manufacturer page could be reached.

devices.notes: Switchcraft documents name the three positions (F, H, N) but do not spell out the signal flow; the behaviour below follows Samson's S-Patch Plus manual and Neutrik's patch panel catalog definitions. F (full normal): with no cord, the top-rear output feeds the bottom-rear input; a plug in the top jack takes the output and breaks the link, and a plug in the bottom jack feeds the input and also breaks it. H (half normal): a plug in the top jack takes a parallel copy without breaking the link (monitoring/split), while a plug in the bottom jack breaks the link. N (non-normal): top and bottom are independent; nothing reaches the bottom row unless a cord is patched. Grounds are set separately with the strap/isolate switches. The DB25 count is not stated by Switchcraft; one Reverb listing (search snippet) counts 12.

devices.notes: Bittree's schematic sheet shows Full Normal, Half Normal and Non-Normal, each combined with bussed, isolated, looped or switched grounds; the text does not describe flow, so the following uses the standard definitions (Samson and Neutrik manuals). Full Normal: the top-row source feeds the bottom-row destination until a plug goes into either jack, which breaks the link. Half Normal: a plug in the top jack listens to (splits) the signal without interrupting it; a plug in the bottom jack breaks the link and feeds the destination. Non-Normal: the rows are not linked. The candidate name 'B96DC' appears only in Bittree drawing part numbers (e.g. B96DC-FNABH/E3...), so the current 969a product is recorded here.

devices.notes: Neutrik's product guide defines half normalled bottom row (the default): internal normalling contacts join each top jack to the jack below; a plug in the bottom jack breaks that link, while a plug in the top jack leaves it in place so the signal can be monitored. Half normalled top row is the mirror image. Full normalled breaks the link from either row. Parallel joins both jacks so both rows carry the same signal. Isolated keeps the rows separate. Neutrik warns against the parallel setting, and against other parallel paths in half-normalled setups, for digital signals (impedance mismatch). The manual also notes that the rows share no ground by default, so for phantom-powered mic lines you must wire the S terminals together or patch with a cord.

devices.notes: From the Samson manual. Normal (N): the top-rear signal feeds the bottom-rear jack. A plug in the top front jack breaks the normal and takes the signal, and the bottom front jack then gives direct access to the bottom-rear input. Half-normal (HN), which Samson suggests for console inserts: a plug in the top jack takes the signal without breaking the normal, so you get a split, and a plug in the bottom jack replaces the normalled feed. Thru (T): each rear jack goes straight to its own front jack and top and bottom are never linked (for sources such as CD players or tie lines). Samson advises against patching microphone outputs through it.

devices.notes: Neutrik ships the card half normalled bottom row. With no cord, each top jack feeds the jack below. A plug in the grey jack always isolates the top row from the bottom row, while a plug in the other jack (Neutrik's front jack A, for 'listening') takes a copy without breaking the link. Turning the PCB gives the 'Turned' configuration. Our reading of the diagrams is that it moves the breaking jack to the other row; Neutrik does not state this in words. The NYS-SPCR1 split card handles send/return on one stereo jack and is suggested as an alternative to a Y-cable for console inputs. No full-normal or thru version is documented. Grounds are set separately with clips. Neutrik states the panel does not handle phantom power.

devices.notes: This panel has no normalling. A cord plugged into a front XLR is connected only to the cable on the XLR directly behind it, so the panel behaves like a non-normalled (thru) patch point. Canare's page calls the XJ3 adapters 'jack to jack' and 'XLR3 full compatible' but does not publish the pin wiring; a 1-1/2-2/3-3 straight wiring is assumed and must be checked against the gated drawing. devices.notes: From Canare's jack charts. On a W (normal-through) jack with no plug, the signal runs from the top rear BNC to the bottom rear BNC. A plug in the upper front port takes the source and terminates the lower BNC in 75 Ω. A plug in the lower port feeds the destination and terminates the upper BNC. Plugs in both ports give through-patching in either direction. On an S (straight-through) jack, the two halves are independent and each unused side is terminated. This is normalled behaviour, with self-termination in place of an open circuit. Two-source check: canare.com gives 'DC to 3.0GHz greater than 10dB Return Loss', which is consistent with the 10 dB at 3 GHz on canare.co.jp. AES-3id is not listed by Canare for this model.
